title: Recent Advances in Experimental Models to Study Endotheliopathy in Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers: Relevance to Lassa Virus
content: Endothelial cells are a common target of several viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHF), including those caused by Lassa virus (LASV) and Ebola virus, yet whether endothelial infection drives the endotheliopathy underlying vascular leakage, coagulopathy and inflammation in severe VHF remains unclear. Understanding these mechanisms requires experimental approaches that adequately capture the complexity of the vascular microenvironment. Here, we review recent experimental advances in understanding endothelial involvement in VHF pathogenesis, with a focus on LASV and complementary recent evidence from other VHFs. We discuss endothelial cell infection in non-human primates and in vitro, immune-endothelial crosstalk, and the effects of soluble or surface-exposed viral proteins on endothelial barrier integrity. Although experimental evidence for LASV-induced endothelial cell activation and barrier dysfunction remains limited, we propose that direct endothelial infection alone is insufficient to account for increased vascular permeability during Lassa fever. Drawing on mechanistic insights from other VHFs, we discuss potential contributions of immune-endothelial interactions, including IL-6 trans-signaling, and soluble or surface-exposed viral proteins to vascular dysfunction during Lassa fever. Furthermore, we review recent advances in organ-on-chip and organoid technologies for modeling the human vasculature and investigating barrier function in the context of VHFs, considering the practical biosafety constraints of high-containment laboratories. Finally, we highlight experimental and methodological priorities for improving the physiological relevance and standardization of these models to enable future mechanistic studies of VHF-associated endotheliopathy.
